Q: How do I create a custom tooltip where trigger=axis with echarts4r? A:

This question should have being posted in the standard "troubleshooting/debugging" category.

If you want to use your synthesized column year_method that you passed to e_charts as bind, it will appear in the tooltip parameter as .name, so your tooltip js formatter can be as simple as this:

e_tooltip(trigger = "axis", formatter = htmlwidgets::JS("
   params=>params.map(
      param=>param.marker+' '+param.name+': '+param.value[1]
   ).join('<br>')
"))

Q: URLImage.createMaskAdapter() / Image.createMask() fails on iOS with moderately sized masks A:

This is a regression due to the recent SIMD optimization. To workaround that try:

Image.setSimdOptimizationsEnabled(false);

We're working on a fix, not sure if it will land in today's release but we'll try. The gist of it is that in order to improve masking performance we're using stack RAM as scratch to perform the masking operation. This works great for smaller images but once you have a larger image we don't have enough room on the stack for the temporary data and we fail.

Q: AVAudioConverter Opus A:

Here's an approach for Opus encoding/decoding with echo cancellation using CoreAudio.

  1. Make two AudioConverterRefs (one for encoding to Opus, one for decoding to lpcm) using your AudioStreamBasicDescriptions. In your code you're using AVAudioConverters but I haven't had luck with these.

  2. For the encoding AudioConverterRef, use AudioConverterSetProperty (or maybe AudioCodecSetProperty, I forgot which class wraps which) to set kAudioCodecPropertyBitRateControlMode. If you set the bit rate mode as constant or long-term average, you should also set kAudioCodecPropertyCurrentTargetBitRate. For example, in a VoIP application, you may want to set a constant bitrate. Read more in the AudioCodec.h header.

  3. Create class properties AVAudioEngine and AVAudioPlayerNode. Make sure all your objects stay alive if using ARC.

  4. Attach the player node to your audio engine.

  5. Turn on voice processing on your audio engine's inputNode using setVoiceProcessingEnabled. This will turn on hardware echo cancellation. Note that voice processing is reliable only when used on the built-in mic/speaker pair on ex. MacBook.

  6. Connect the player node to your audio engine. Verify my order of steps is consistent with the example in documentation.

  7. Get your audio engine's inputNode's output format (using outputFormatForBus). This will be the format coming from your mic. Since voice processing is enabled, you'll have extra channels. See my other answer for more info. The relevant fields in the mic format are commonFormat, sampleRate, channelCount. Also, get your audio engine's outputNode's input format (using inputFormatForBus). This is the format going to your speaker.

  8. Make an AVAudioConverter to change the mic format as needed. Likely, you'll need to change bitdepth from Float32 to Int16, sampleRate (not needed in your case), and channel count using the converter's channelMap property (see my answer linked above). Your channelMap likely needs to look like @[@0] which takes the first channel from your mic and ignores the rest.

  9. Set up a tap on your inputNode using installTapOnBus. Set bufferSize based on your mic format's sampleRate and the tap frequency. Supported values of the tap frequency are [100,400] ms so for reducing VoIP latency, use 100ms. For example, if your mic format has 48khz sampleRate, the bufferSize should be 4800. Set format to the mic format from step 7.

  10. Within the tap block, use the AVAudioConverter from step 8 to change the format. Ensure that the destination buffer for the conversion has the right frame capacity ex. if converting from 48->16khz the destination frame capacity is 1600 (in your case, no sampleRate change).

  11. Break up your converted buffer into chunks, where each chunk maps to a single Opus packet. For example, your Opus packets are likely 20ms, which for 16khz is 320 bytes per chunk.

  12. Use AudioConverterFillComplexBuffer with the right AudioConverterRef to encode each chunk to a single Opus packet. Read the documentation on this function as well as AudioConverterComplexInputDataProc. Basically, AudioConverterRef will call this DataProc as needed to pull data for conversion. Since we're telling the converter to give a single Opus packet, it will only call the DataProc once. You provide everything the DataProc needs via inUserData which is a user-defined struct. Within the DataProc, you modify the fields of ioData to point to the data you got in your user-defined struct. Also, the converter may ask for input packet description via outDataPacketDescription. It likely won't ask for the encoding side, but will ask for the decoding side. In this case, you must pass in the packet description via your user-defined struct. Your AudioStreamPacketDescription for decoding is straightforward, provide the size, start offset = 0, and variable frames = 0 (assuming your Opus packets are standard ex. 16khz 20ms per packet).

  13. Now that you have your encoded Opus packet, we're done!

For the decoding side.

  1. Use similar logic to step 12 from above on the other AudioConverterRef to decode each Opus packet into a lpcm chunk.

  2. Make an AVAudioConverter and use similar logic to step 8 from above to convert your lpcm chunk to match the speaker format found in step 7. Your channelMap here likely needs to look like @[@0, @0] which takes your single channel decoded audio and copies it to both channels (for stereo speaker output). Again, make sure your destination frame capacity is correct (step 10).

  3. Now that you have your decoded lpcm chunk, schedule at the player node with scheduleBuffer.

  4. Finally, if (!self.playerNode.playing) { [self.playerNode play]; }
